title: Wolfspeed Commercializes Transparent Silicon Carbide Substrates for Quantum Computing and Integrated Photonics - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Wolfspeed has commercially launched optical-grade transparent silicon carbide (TSiC) wafers at 150 mm and 200 mm, with 300 mm sampling. They were first aimed at AR waveguides and are now being pitched to quantum hardware as a host for spin qubits and integrated photonics. QCR frames this as a challenge to synthetic diamond, which cannot scale to fab-size wafers, though smart-cut thin-film transfer and isotopic purity remain hurdles.

insights.claim: Wolfspeed launched its optical-grade transparent silicon carbide (TSiC) wafers commercially at 150 mm and 200 mm, with 300 mm wafers sampling. The product was first targeted at AR near-eye display waveguides and is now offered across the quantum hardware supply chain.

insights.claim: Single-crystal 4H-SiC hosts optically addressable spin defects, such as divacancies and silicon vacancies, that have long coherence times and emit near the telecom O- and C-bands. Its high refractive index and thermal conductivity allow spin qubits, waveguides and photon routing to be built in the same crystal layer.

insights.claim: Optical-grade SiC directly challenges synthetic diamond as the main host for color-center quantum hardware. Diamond NV centers are mature, but diamond is limited to small-area mosaics that cannot scale on 200 mm or 300 mm fab lines, while 200 mm SiC works with standard DUV lithography and plasma etching.

insights.so_what: Wafer scale could shift solid-state quantum hardware from diamond to SiC.

insights.claim: Low-loss SiC-on-insulator photonics requires perfecting smart-cut thin-film transfer without lattice damage that quenches spin-defect emission. Cryogenic optical coherence also requires depleting 29Si and 13C isotopes to suppress spectral diffusion and nuclear-spin dephasing.

insights.so_what: Having substrates available does not yet make fault-tolerant processors, so commercial quantum revenue for Wolfspeed is likely far off.
